newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy hopes to turn EU confusion to own advantage.
newsitem.headline: Italy hopes to turn EU confusion to own advantage.

text.p: Italy has barely been able to hide its delight at the turmoil within the heart of the European Union, confident that German budget woes and French unemployment concerns have boosted its own single currency credentials.

"The fanaticism for accountancy, that until now has strongly conditioned the path to monetary union, has been cracked," Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco said after the French questioned a stability pact designed to enforce fiscal restraint in Europe.

The apparent tilt in EU political thinking over recent days, away from purely fiscal rigour and towards themes such as job creation, will help Italy's chances of becoming a founder member of economic and monetary union (EMU), analysts said.

But they warned that it was in Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi's interests not to let the shift in economic emphasis tilt too far, saying Rome would be the big loser if the perceived change of direction in European circles put a brake on EMU.
"It would be crazy to think Italian financial markets would not suffer if EMU was delayed," said Giovanna Mossetti, chief economist at Milan brokers Caboto.
Perhaps aware of this, Prodi has already urged his French counterpart Lionel Jospin to sign the stability pact at next week's Amsterdam summit of EU leaders.

Italian debt instruments have risen strongly over the past year and interest rates have fallen as the centre-left government made great strides to meet most of the criteria established in the Maastricht Treaty for EMU hopefuls.

Since taking office in May 1996, Prodi has introduced around 100 trillion lire ($59.2 billion) of cuts and savings in a bid to slash the state deficit to the required three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 from 6.7 percent in 1996.

Rome has been criticised by many for introducing a host of one-off measures as part of its budget battle, and despite some creative accounting, a state-funded research body predicted this week that Italy would just miss the three percent goal.

But with both the German government and the new socialist administration in Paris struggling to make the grade, Italy is convinced it will have done enough to win a strong negotiating position when EMU founder members are chosen next year.
"We are no longer bottom of the class," Visco said.
Italian confidence has also been lifted by French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's pledge to have a wide pool of countries in EMU, including Italy, from the word go in January 1999.
"As I have repeatedly said...Europe is not just about the economy and the economy is not just about the currency," Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told parliament on Wednesday.

This confidence has been reflected in the market, with a recent Reuter's poll of 47 economists and political analysts across Europe showing 45 percent of respondents seeing Italy in the first EMU wave versus a mere 14 percent in May.

"Italy's EMU chances have improved," said Riccardo Barbieri, senior economist with Morgan Stanley in London. "But there is always the possibility that Italy could be sacrificed on the altar of Franco-German relations," he added.

German public opinion is deeply opposed to letting Italy join the single European currency from the start, with the national debt so high (more than 120 percent of GDP) and state spending still not fully tamed.
To calm these fears, Italy must produce a convincing reform of the welfare state later this autumn, as promised, and introduce a solid 1998 budget, analysts said.
"This would not only bolster Italy's EMU bid, but if EMU cracked later on...it would also protect Italy from the fallout," Barbieri said. $1 = 1,670 lire
